title: Client SDK lazy-schema and tool-routing proposal
content:
Summary

This is a working PRD sketch for a new Hosted API surface and client SDK ergonomics that focuses on: incremental (progressive) delivery of structured outputs, a lightweight lazy-schema negotiation model, and a client-side-first tool-routing hint protocol. The goal is to make low-latency, partially-structured responses simple to consume while enabling reliable tool calling and graceful fallback behavior.

Audience
- Frontend engineers building UI experiences that render partial output as it arrives (chat, code assist, search snippets).
- Backend/Platform engineers integrating tool-call orchestration (retrievers, external actions) into a single API call.
- SDK authors who must balance ergonomics, backpressure and small-bundle size for browser clients.

Problem statement
- Current streaming outputs are token-oriented and opaque: clients receive raw text diffs and have to parse/interpret structured payloads themselves. That makes tool-calling and structured updates brittle and latency-heavy when clients need to wait for full JSON blobs.
- When model-based tool calls are required, routing decisions (which external tool to call) currently happen server-side with limited client visibility, making debugging and deterministic fallback hard.
- SDK ergonomics are inconsistent: heavyweight parsers, unclear retry semantics, and awkward buffers for progressive rendering.

Design goals
1) Progressive structured delivery: support incremental emission of typed deltas so clients can render/act on partial structured outputs safely.
2) Lazy-schema negotiation: avoid requiring the client to know full output schema upfront; support on-demand schema patches and small typed descriptors.
3) Explicit tool-routing hints: a lightweight channel for the model to recommend (and the server to assert) which tool(s) should be invoked, with confidence scores and fallback plans.
4) Minimal SDK surface: a few composable primitives that work in node/browser with predictable backpressure and telemetry hooks.
5) Backwards-compatible: fall back to existing token streams and full JSON blobs when clients/servers are not upgraded.

Non-goals
- We are not designing a full RPC format or replacing OpenAPI for tool endpoints. This is about in-band hints and progressive structured frames, not endpoint definition.
- Not attempting to canonicalize all schema types; we aim for a lean contract that supports common patterns (objects, arrays, typed events).

High-level approach
- Streaming transport: SSE or WebSocket carry a sequence of typed "delta frames." Each frame is a small JSON object (type: text|update|schema|tool_hint|end|error) wrapped in an SSE/data message. Text frames maintain current token stream. Update frames carry partial structured payloads as path-qualified diffs (a la JSON Patch lite). Schema frames carry small type descriptors (field names, expected primitives, enums) keyed by schema id. Tool_hint frames carry {tool_id, confidence, inputs, fallback_chain}.
- Lazy-schema negotiation: the server includes schema ids and minimal descriptors only when needed. Clients can request (via a control frame) a richer descriptor for a schema id if they intend to validate or render typed widgets.
- Tool-routing orchestration: tool_hint frames do not directly invoke tools. They represent the model's recommendation. The server-side orchestrator maps tool_hint -> tool invocation using config (customer routing table). The response stream includes a tool_event frame with invocation result or a failure event and optional fallback tool_hint.

API sketch (server <> client frames)
- Open stream: POST /v1/streams with body {model, prompt, capabilities: ["progressive_structured", "tool_hints"]} -> 200 with session_id.
- Streaming frames (SSE format):
  - data: {"type":"text","seq":12,"text":"Hello"}
  - data: {"type":"update","seq":13,"path":"/response/choices/0","patch":{"title":"Draft"}}
  - data: {"type":"schema","schema_id":"s_42","desc":{"title":{"type":"string"},"items":{"type":"array","items":{"$ref":"s_7"}}}}
  - data: {"type":"tool_hint","tool_id":"search_v1","confidence":0.93,"inputs":{"query":"best routing for sdk"}}
  - data: {"type":"tool_event","tool_id":"search_v1","status":"invoked","event_id":"e_678"}
  - data: {"type":"tool_event","tool_id":"search_v1","status":"result","event_id":"e_678","result_path":"/response/tools/search_v1/0"}
  - data: {"type":"end","final":true}

Note: all frames are small; text continues to stream even while updates and tool_events interleave. Clients must be able to process frames out-of-band.

Client SDK ergonomics (proposed primitives)
- StreamClient.open(opts) -> StreamHandle with events: onText(callbackChunk), onUpdate(callbackPatch), onToolEvent(callback), onSchema(schemaId, descriptor), onEnd().
- StreamHandle.requestSchema(schema_id) -> Promise<descriptor> (server may respond with schema frame or inline descriptor).
- StreamHandle.setBackpressureBudget(tokens:number) -> informs server-side batching policy via control channel; SDK enforces that it will hold parsing/rendering if budget exhausted.
- StreamHandle.ackToolEvent(event_id, decision) -> explicit ack for long-running tool actions (accept result, ask for re-run, fallback).

Examples (browser-friendly)
- Minimal usage (progressive text + partial structured title)
  const s = StreamClient.open({model:'rwd-m', capabilities:['progressive_structured']});
  s.onText(t => appendToChat(t));
  s.onUpdate(patch => applyPatchToState(patch));
  s.onEnd(() => enableSendButton());

- Tool-aware usage
  s.onToolEvent(e => {
    if (e.status === 'result') {
      // apply into state at e.result_path
      applyPatchToState({path: e.result_path, patch: e.result});
    }
  });

Structured format details
- Base representation: small JSON objects with a path and a patch. Patch semantics are intentionally restricted: set, append, remove. No arbitrary nested operations to keep client cost low.
- Schema descriptors: intentionally tiny (field name, type, optional enum values). Complex types can reference other schema_ids. That keeps first-frame payloads small and lets clients lazily request full descriptors only when rendering typed widgets.
- Versioning: schema_id is opaque and stable for the duration of a session. Servers may emit schema_version frames if a type evolves mid-session.

Tool orchestration and fallback playbook
- Tool_hint is advisory. Server maps to a concrete invocation via customer routing rules. The streaming responses will include tool_event frames for invocation lifecycle.
- Fallback rules: each tool_hint may include a fallback_chain: [toolA, toolB, builtin_stub]. If a tool fails or times out, server emits a new tool_hint with lower confidence or a tool_event with status 'failed' plus recommended fallback.
- Client involvement: clients can optionally ack tool_event and indicate preference for stale vs fresh results, or escalate to server for synchronous blocking of stream until tool completes. This is opt-in to preserve low latency for progressive UIs.

Telemetry and observability
- Each stream includes metadata: session_id, route_hint, model_version, and token_count so Console can break down token-level cost and latencies per-frame type.
- SDK emits local telemetry hooks: onFrameLatency(type,ms), onBackpressureApplied, toolEventLatency(tool_id,ms). These are surfaced to Redwood Console as optional telemetry.

Compatibility and fallback
- If client does not request progressive_structured capability, server falls back to classic token SSE (data: text tokens) and final JSON in the end frame.
- If a client requests schema but server does not support it, server responds with a single schema frame with type:"unsupported". SDK should gracefully degrade to text-only mode.

Migration plan (phases)
1) Internal dogfooding: implement server frame generation and basic node SDK in internal beta for Console templates. Track real-product UX improvements for chat and code assist (2–4 weeks).
2) Public SDK alpha (browser + node): expose StreamClient primitives, full examples, opt-in by capability flags. Add telemetry hooks and JIT schema endpoint. (4–6 weeks).
3) Customer pilot: partner with two customers building progressive UIs; iterate on schema descriptor shapes and fallback ergonomics (6–8 weeks).
4) GA: add policy controls in Console, SLA notes, and migration guide for existing streaming clients (3 months after pilot).

Open questions / Risks
- How large should schema descriptors be before they harm first-byte latency? (measure with microbenchmarks)
- Should we standardize the patch format (JSON Patch subset) or invent a smaller custom diff format? Tradeoffs between complexity and client CPU.
- Security: tool_hint content could leak PII if model hallucinated a tool name. Need server-side validation and a safe allowlist.
- Rate of schema evolution: if models change schemas mid-session, clients may get inconsistent patches. Consider pinning schema per session or emitting clear schema_version frames.
- Backpressure semantics: defining the server's reaction to client budget signals needs careful calibration to avoid starvation or thundering.

Next steps (short-term)
- Engineering spike: implement small server-side generator that emits text+update+tool_hint frames for an internal model. Measure 95th percentile first-byte and end-to-end tool_event latency. (ENG-2748)
- SDK spike: prototype StreamClient primitives in the JS SDK, focusing on small bundle size and graceful degradation. (PR: github.com.../pull/783)
- Product: draft a short migration guide for existing streaming clients and a Console UI spec for per-route schema inspection.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally a lightweight, iterative proposal. Expect the first iteration to be conservative in schema richness to prioritize byte/latency budgets. Please comment on tradeoffs and raise any regulatory/privacy concerns for tool_hint content.

Scratchpad / brainstorming fragments
- idea: UI widgets can subscribe to schema_id and render skeletons while waiting for typed updates. Good UX for forms inside chat cards.
- TODO: confirm SSE vs websocket perf differences in browser with small payloads (2–64B frames).
- Slack threads: #sdk-streaming, thread ts 1689201023 (see linked slack message)

End of draft.
